segments.expected: She told him on the boards by the draft board, with the timber pond lying black beside them and the gate mast standing over Noa's empty desk. She did not tell him all of it. She told him that she dreamed with a fever, and had since she was thirteen. It was the thing in Annick's notebook and the Ferren keeper's book and the keeper's book at the pump house here, on the same night in 2604. Her aunt had written it down the same night last spring, in her words, and had it sealed before she read anybody else's. And she meant to stand up at the Salt Hall at seven and ask the Board to open the page.

segments.expected: "Three," said the marshal. "And a down. Four to the Ropewalk."
segments.transcript: Three, said the marshal, and a down. Four, to the rope walk.

segments.expected: She had seen it. She had seen it from her knees, a pace off, with her shoulder still warm where the edge had touched. Carrow had not looked at the litter. She had not looked at Jude. She had walked down the pen with her eyes on nothing and her edge lit, and she had brought it down when Treen spoke and not a hair before. Treen had been watching Jude's hands. When Jude's hands went north, Treen said set, and Carrow came down on the nearest thing she could reach, which had been Kiva.

segments.expected: They walked. They walked the Commodore down the north side of the pen, close against the posts, on their arms, as two washerwomen walk a basket between them. Behind them Anwen had stopped leaning. Lyle was planted two paces off her wall with her shoulder against it, leaning from the floor, and Anwen walked the far end of her wall round. She did not push the near end. She walked the far end in a quarter circle, slowly, as Mace had taught her on a van's line at home, and the near end came after it.

segments.expected: Kiva knelt. She had to shut and let go to kneel, and the moment she let go of the poles Tolver had them. He did not lift. He held the head, and Lyle came off Anwen's wall, and the two still doors took the Commodore by the poles together and walked him back down the pen as two men carry a sleeping friend upstairs. Carrow walked beside them with her edge lit. Jude went for Tolver's back and Treen said hands and Carrow's edge came round between them, and Jude stopped, because the alternative was to walk into it.

segments.expected: Lyle leaned on a wall that was no longer where she was leaning. She leaned on air, from the floor, with her feet planted and all her weight coming up through her heels, and there was nothing there.
segments.transcript: Lyle leaned on a wall that was no longer where she was leaning. She leaned on air from the floor, with her feet planted and all her weight coming up through her heels, and there was nothing there.

segments.expected: She did not go to the pump house to ask him anything at first. She went because it was the slack, and the Board's sitting was at seven, and she had never in her life stood up in a hall full of strangers and asked to be heard about a thing that was not a door, and she wanted to stand somewhere quiet first. The pump house's outfall walk was the only quiet place she knew in Saltmere. For twenty minutes twice a day, if a ruined hand was right, it was the only quiet place in the town.
